We provide an updated version of the enumerative information related to the family of lines that intersect a triple of hypersurfaces within a well-defined polynomial scenario. Originally, this count was intended to equal half of the third Pontrjagin class's top degree coefficient, but our re-examination reveals a different result. Nonetheless, we connect this count to the third Pontrjagin class's top degree coefficient, but in a more complex manner. This involves a specific projective minimality condition and a particular triple of hypersurfaces, leading to the sought-after relationship.

SN 2020jfo was a hydrogen-rich supernova that exploded in 2020 and was observed until it disappeared from view in 2021.  We used a extensive library of approximately 160 supernovae spectra and 13 broadband colors to study the remarkable characteristics of SN 2020jfo.  Although its peak luminosity was modest, its plateau phase was unusually long, taking six weeks to fade.  We propose a theoretical framework to explain its prolonged plateau phase, and it matches the characteristics of Type II supernovae commonly found in young galaxies.  The amount of ejected material was likely substantial, and SN 2020jfo may have appeared briefly as a nebular supernova before its gradual fade.

To greatly decrease the footprint of monitoring surveys in X-ray observations, increasing the field of view (FOV) of detectors is a crucial strategy. To achieve this, we're exploring the combination of lobster-eye (LE) optics, which offer a unique capability for wide-angle observations. By integrating multiple LE mirrors, we're capable of achieving an FOV of up to 7.5 x 10^-3 steradians, a significant improvement over the 2.6 steradians provided by a single LE mirror. To optimize the performance for detecting point sources, we've developed a model for the modulation transfer function of an array of LE mirrors and calculated the minimum detectable flux of a proposed X-ray telescope employing this optics configuration. According to our calculations, this telescope could identify a source with a 2.5 sigma confidence at an energy of 1 keV within an FOV of 7.5 x 10^-3 steradians in just 1000 s with a photon collection efficiency of approximately 0.3. To achieve this, we propose using an array of 36 x 36 LE mirrors, with an edge length of 2 mm, and separating them by 100 micrometers to minimize diffraction effects.

We establish the optimal bound for a specific type of averaging operator known as the Stech general stage set operator, which applies when the underlying surface has a specific smoothness property and includes curved surfaces. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of this result in the context of a particular type of elliptic obstacle problem characerized by local minimal surface assumptions and bounded exterior angles.

Researchers have found that dark matter halo shapes are often randomly distributed, which may indicate a violation of Einstein's general relativity at a cosmic scale. To better understand the relationship between dark matter halo shapes and the matter distribution around them, this paper uses artificial neural networks to analyze the distribution of dark matter halo shapes and velocities. By training a neural network on simulated dark matter halo samples, it was able to replicate the same random shape distribution. When the network was applied to real-world data, it was able to accurately predict the velocity of dark matter halos based on their shapes, which in turn revealed that hairy haloes are less common than expected. This insight could be a result of an underlying cosmological parameter, which the paper leaves for further investigation. Alternatively, it may provide a way to directly link velocity dispersion to the matter distribution around dark matter haloes.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method involves using a formulation that combines the Lagrangian formalism with the use of conformally flat space-time, and we have taken steps to ensure that our approach is consistent with the laws of physics. Our methodology involves modifying the metric in a way that depends on the mass function, and we have explicitly provided the modified metric in our papers from 2005 and 2006, where we detailed the specifics of our approach. Building on this foundation, we have developed a numerical code to solve for rotating star configurations using a Lagrangian formalism, and our code allows for a wide range of masses, including primordial and post-merger objects, as well as stars with substantial amounts of neutron star matter. Through our simulations, we have obtained reliable solutions for rotating stars across various mass ranges, and our results match previous findings from the Komatsu-Erigene-Sato code, which used a different approach based on the Bondi gauge.

A major challenge in creating AI document extraction systems lies in manually labeling large amounts of data, which often hinders the development and deployment of these systems. To overcome this issue, we explore whether few labeled documents can be effectively combined with a vast amount of unlabeled data to train more accurate and generalizable models. To address this challenge, we designed a novel approach called Visually-rich Document Extraction via Transfer Learning (VDET). First, we train a base model on a small set of labeled documents. Then, we fine-tune this base model on a large set of unlabeled documents with the same class structure. To accommodate documents without a clear class structure, we use a more general document extraction task without classification. In both cases, we achieve significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the benefits of VDET. Moreover, VDET allows for the scalable incorporation of unlabeled documents, enabling the application to be seamlessly transferred to different domains. We also show that VDET can be successfully applied to multiple challenging document extraction tasks, including extracting key information from invoices, receipts, and medical bills, without prior knowledge of their format.

The imminent generation of kilohertz-band gravitational waves from merging compact binaries holds great promise for detecting binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole events. However, distinguishing between these events and identifying the composition of the colliding binaries can be challenging using traditional matched filtering analysis. To overcome this, we explored the use of deep learning models to identify the object composition and categorize events into specific binary types. Utilizing a large database of simulated signals for neutron star-neutron star, neutron star-black hole, and black hole-black hole events, we trained a multi-task deep learning model to accurately classify signals by object composition and binary type. Our results demonstrate that this model efficiently distinguishes between different binary types and accurately identifies the composition of the colliding binaries. Interestingly, using a trained feature extractor, we found that the deep learning model's ability to classify signals relies on the signal's frequency content rather than its match with a predicted waveform. Consequently, this approach allows for the analysis of a broader range of signals beyond those employed in our training data.

Urban residents' social interactions are a key aspect of urban functioning and are influenced by various factors, including physical distancing measures implemented during the pandemic. Researchers used a mixed-methods approach, combining statistical analysis of public transportation passenger data and qualitative interviews with transportation workers, to explore the impact of pandemic restrictions on urban social interactions in Tokyo and Tama. The study found that physical distancing measures significantly reduced public transportation passengers in Tokyo and Tama. Although restrictions were eased in late May and resumed in late July, passengers in Tokyo returned to pre-pandemic levels more slowly than in Tama. Qualitative interviews with transportation workers revealed that workers in Tama experienced increased anxiety about infections and financial difficulties in Tokyo, with some workers in Tama reporting a decline in passengers of up to 50%. In contrast, workers in Tokyo reported a decrease in passengers of around 20-30%. Notably, reductions in social interactions varied significantly across different income groups, with low-income groups exhibiting a 12% decrease in interactions, whereas middle- and high-income groups exhibited increases of 3% and 5% respectively. Notably, pre-pandemic low-income groups had the fewest urban interactions. Consequently, the pandemic exacerbated income disparities in urban interactions.

We present detailed models of a massive young protostellar object (MYSO) whose growth is influenced by accretion and mergers in the surrounding disk. Observational evidence, including a strong spectral line shift and a highly luminous infrared spectrum, suggests that the MYSO, known as CYX CB54, is in a stage where it is accumulating material from a surrounding disk and engaging in protostar-proststar mergers. 

Using a combination of radiative hydro dynamics simulations and post-processing spectral synthesis, we compared our predicted spectral signatures from CYX CB54 with existing data and found that its growth is likely rapid, with the MYSO accumulating 0.25 solar masses per 10,000 years as a result of both accretion and mergers. 

Furthermore, we found that CYX CB54 is undergoing multiple mergers with small, low-mass objects, including some that result in the formation of massive jets. These models are in agreement with existing observational evidence, including the presence of large molecular clumps and dense prestellar cores in the surrounding environment. 

Our analysis also revealed that CYX CB54 is a young object with an age of less than 50,000 years, and its growth is likely a transient phase lasting no more than 30,000 years. Moreover, we found that CYX CB54 is a member of a binary or multiple star system, with at least one companion that is a low-mass star or small disk

This research develops a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation to model weakly nonlinear deep-water gravity waves with uniform vorticity in a rotating system, where the amplitude is assumed to be small when compared to the wavelength. The primary distinction between this and existing Dysthe equation formulations, which account for rectilinear wave grouping effects, lies in the inclusion of both stationary and translating uniform vortices. The resulting Hamiltonian Dysthe formulation preserves the Hamiltonian nature of the underlying Hamiltonian system and leads to a Dysthe equation formulation that accounts for both the effects of dispersiveness and vorticity. The resulting Dysthe equation formulation can be seen as a linearization of the Hamiltonian system in a Hamiltonian sense, which enables us to apply nonlinear Hamiltonian modeling tools to study the Dysthe equation's solutions and associated statistics.

We start by reviewing the basis construction given in [13, chapter 7] and modify it to suit locally arching spaces. This results in a modified basis with which we can perform a change of variables and apply Stokes' theorem to locally arching spaces.

Autonomous navigation in complex indoor environments with low-ceiling spaces and temperature gradients is a challenging task for mobile robots. To overcome these difficulties, this research focuses on incorporating a sophisticated navigation system that utilizes a low-cost sonar sensor in real-time while accounting for the effects of temperature fluctuations on air density and subsequent impact on acoustic signal propagation. By drawing upon theoretical models of thermodynamics and acoustics, this study develops a precise framework to calculate the variance in sonar readings caused by temperature changes and plumes of rising warm air. To integrate this sensor data effectively, a nonlinear Kalman filter is employed to provide a precise estimation of the robot's position while taking into consideration the variability and bias in the sonar sensor readings. Through extensive simulation and actual testing in an office environment, this navigation system is proven to be highly efficient and accurate in providing a reliable path for the robot to follow.

The veracity of online news poses a significant challenge in today's information-rich environment. False news spreads quickly online due to its simplicity and engaging nature, but it frequently causes trouble and credit loss for both individuals and the wider community. To address this issue, automatic false news detection techniques are being developed and implemented. These methods typically employ deep learning models, which, although highly accurate, are associated with several drawbacks due to their substantial computational requirements and necessity for extensive datasets. This paper proposes a two-component system to address the veracity of online news. First, a pre-filtering component employs a convolutional neural network to classify the veracity of social media news based on low-dimensional embedded representations. To enhance the effectiveness of this component, the text of news articles is condensed into a more compact form using a latent semantic analysis-based method. This compacted text enhances the component's performance by providing a more precise embedded representation. This paper's approach was tested on a large dataset of 24,582 news articles, spanning nine categories, and yielded a 93% accuracy rate.

This research investigates how geometric properties, specifically curvature, influence Gaussian stochastic fields. It begins by introducing Gaussian stochastic fields and their associated Hessian matrices, then reviews the existing literature on their expected sectional curvature. Building on this foundation, we calculate the expected sectional curvature of a specific class of Gaussian stochastic fields defined by a Laplace operator and determine its overall regularity. Additionally, the study compares these fields to natural analogues defined by the Laplace-Beltrami operator, examining their equivalence in a mean square sense.

We investigate a specialized instance of linear dimensionality reduction that involves finding the principal component of a data set in the $\ell_1$-norm space, specifically for data sets with rotational symmetry. We show that using the median absolute deviation method, we can determine this component in a way that yields a linearly convergent outcome.

Deep-learning-based models, especially BERT, have consistently delivered superior performance   in natural language processing tasks.  This study investigates whether BERT can be trained to accurately   identify and modify semantic tags in the Stanford Dependency Parse dataset, which is commonly   used to represent sentence semantics.  To examine this capability, we combined the semantic tags   with the Dependency Parse dataset, using a method called Tag-Dep, which has not been previously   established in the literature.  To validate this Tag-Dep format, we utilized a multiple-choice   emotion-connected question dataset that links text to emotion categories.  Our results indicate   that both raw BERT and a trained sentiment BERT model excel at emitting original semantic tags,   while only raw BERT demonstrates proficiency in adjusting semantic tags.  Furthermore, both   versions of BERT exhibit high accuracy in labeling the Tag-Dep format with correct emotion   categories.  Our findings suggest that BERT can be trained to accurately identify and modify   semantic tags, and the Tag-Dep format is a effective means of conveying sentence semantics   that is readily understandable by BERT.

For robots to effectively navigate complex, indoor environments with limited mapping information, a new method called HiTMap has been developed. This approach involves creating a unique, hierarchical graph-based map representation that is both distilled from sparse landmarks and prioritizes critical path information. In contrast to conventional mapping techniques that rely on extensive floor plan data and extensive exploration, HiTMap enables a robot to generate a representative map in as little as 10 minutes, using only a minimal set of landmarks detected via a monocular camera. Through rigorous simulation testing of a representative indoor office space, HiTMap navigation performance was found to surpass that of a state-of-the-art slam algorithm by a margin of at least 25%. Additionally, HiTMap's cost and computational requirements were determined to be significantly lower than that of the slam algorithm, paving the way for its potential applications in energy-constrained, indoor navigation tasks.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields within an atomic interferometry system that contains a moving atomic component.  Due to the fragile nature of interference patterns, even minor shifts in the atomic trajectory, resulting from magnetic field-induced Casimir forces in atomic layers, could potentially impede the measurement sensitivity.  However, we show that utilizing a specific atomic interferometry setup, where the light is directed perpendicular to the atomic propagation, allows for the conversion of momentum shifts into spatial shifts, enabling the measurement of extremely weak local magnetic fields, down to values of $10^{-3}$G, which also correlates with the magnitude of the atomic mass.  Moreover, this approach enables the precise determination of the atomic interaction with the surrounding environment, including the strength of the atomic layer's response to the Meissner effect, which could pave the way for novel applications in low-field magnetometry, as well as an atomic-scale analysis of the Casimir self-sticking phenomenon.

A mixture model contains a mixture model as a special case where a single distribution makes up the entire mixture component. We can think of mixtures as being part of a broader family of models that include mixture models. In this paper, a specific type of model that includes both mixture and mixture model variants is explored. A new algorithm is developed that applies to these more general models and provides an alternative to analysis based on geometric representation. The paper also discusses how models can be distinguished from each other.

High-performance object-based programming in CUDA is hindered by inefficient memory management resulting from manual memory management practices.  To overcome this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator for CUDA that offers both lock-free and lock-coarse-grained allocation and deallocation functionality.  To further optimize memory usage, DynaSOAr employs a just-in-time allocation strategy that prioritizes the use of a small, locally-managed pool of memory.  As a key contribution, we introduce a novel, lock-free fragmentation-reduction mechanism called "coalesced splitting."  To evaluate the performance of DynaSOAr, we conducted a series of benchmarks that demonstrate up to 7x speedup in application performance and highlight the suitability of DynaSOAr for various object-based programming workloads.

A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to describe the spin states of a single manganese adatom and manganese dimers on the Nb(110) surface by accounting for interactions with nearby conduction electrons and localized Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. Based on an initial principles approach, the parameters of the theory were determined through a thorough band structure calculation of the Nb(110) surface. The resulting model exhibits an intricate interplay of superparamagnetism, antiferromagnetism, and ferromagnetism dependent on the spacing between two manganese adatoms. Computational predictions are closely examined and found to conincide with experimental outcomes, and the theoretical framework is versatile enough to be applied to other transition metal adatoms on various substrates.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of three mini-Neptunes with different orbital periods. By analyzing $TESS$ data, we found evidence for three planets with periods of 5.85, 9.84, and 21.8 days, and mass similar to that of Neptune. Further investigation using spectroscopic techniques from the $HARPS$ instrument revealed the star's parameters, including its rotation speed, and confirmed the planets' masses as 6.8, 7.4, and 8.4 times the mass of Earth, respectively. Evaluating the planets' positions relative to their star, we found them to be nearly aligned with the ecliptic plane. Assessing the systems' stability and searching for additional planets in the system using a dynamical model, we found no significant variations. Computing the planets' ages and using the $HARPS$ data, we found them to be 765 million years old, indicating the planets formed during the protoplanetary disk's initial stages. Inspecting the planetary radii and calculating their core sizes, we found them to have core radii similar to that of Neptune. Verifying the planets' atmospheric characteristics using the $B-T$ curve, we found the outer layers to be primarily composed of water with some hydrogen and helium.

We investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defect pairs in rutile TiO2\textsubscript{2} using the VPOS method within the framework of DFT. Our results show that both carbon and nitrogen defects are able to form covalent bonds with neighboring titanium atoms, leading to a sp\textsuperscript{2} hybridization and arrangement of electrons. This, in turn, results in the formation of a magnetic moment at the defect site. However, the magnitude of the magnetic moment depends on the arrangement of the electrons and defects. Our findings also indicate that the distance between defects significantly affects the formation of a piezoelectric field and resulting electric field-induced magnetism. Moreover, the distribution of electrons and resulting magnetic moment changes when a sulfur atom replaces a nitrogen atom, replacing the sp\textsupersuper{2} hybridization with an s\textsuperscript{2}p\textsupersuper{2} arrangement. Our predicted outcomes are compatible with experimental data, and we anticipate that our results will guide the design of materials featuring piezoelectric and magnetic properties.

One of the predominant production processes for top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider involves the combination of a top-quark and a bottom-quark. This process can mask the elastic creation of top-quarks, which would demonstrate that the standard model of particle physics can accommodate both Compton scattering and elastic pair production for heavy particles. To overcome this obstacle, researchers suggest utilizing forward proton detectors in the Large Hadron Collider to identify the elastic production of top-quarks in proton-proton collisions. This would provide the first empirical proof of elastic pair production of heavy particles within the standard model of particle physics.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin established the ground-breaking homogenity of $K_n$ within binomial graphs. This discovery motivated further research into the homogenity of $K_n$ within randomly generated ramsey graphs. Our study focuses on the Ramsey density of $K_n$ within infinite, countably edged graphs and determines a precise homogeneous density value for $K_n$ – namely, its minimal Ramsey density is equivalent to the smallest solution $f$ in the equation $f^2+2f\geq 1$, which equals $1$.

We investigate quantum electrodynamics in (1+1)d space-time using qutrits as a model for massless scalar field theory, focusing on non-perturbative effects in vacuum fluctuations and their impact on the vacuum expectation value of the electric field. Our research reveals that a specific "sound" mode, related to the massless scalar field, exhibits a notable phenomenon where the expectation value of the electric field's square cycles between positive and negative values as the external magnetic field varies. This behavior has been observed in simulations of both small and large magnetic fields. Our results demonstrate that even in the limit of a strong external field, the model maintains consistency with the Wightman function's expected properties. Moreover, we find that the model's choice of boundary conditions has a significant effect on sound mode's properties.

Research indicates that a highly polarized positron beam can be created by directing a high-power laser at a thick foil target, and that the generated positrons exhibit significant polarization properties, particularly within the extreme field quantum electrodynamics regime. As the laser-energy interaction progresses, the degree of positron polarization shows a distinct anisotropy, with up to 40% polarization observed when the electron-positron pair production is heavily saturated. Conversely, in the non-saturated regime, the polarization drops to approximately 10%. Moreover, as the angle between the positron direction and the electric field vector increases, the polarization properties shift to a more sinusoidal dependence, coupled with a significant reduction in polarization, with values as low as 5% recorded.

A function $f$ is considered a limited function within a specific context if it meets two criteria. Firstly, $f$ must adhere to the constraint that the sum of its bits does not exceed a predetermined number, which in this case is described as $g(n)$. Secondly, $f$ must fit within the bounds of another function, namely $h(n)$, when compared in a binary format. When examining functions of this nature, we are able to establish a lower bound on the size of truth tables required to accurately determine the value of $f(g(n)) \mod h(n)$. This lower bound is found to be substantial, with sizes of truth tables needing to be substantial, specifically with an upper limit of $n^{1-\epsilon}$ for any conceivable $\epsilon > 0$. This finding is significant as it addresses an unresolved issue from a previous study.

This research develops a miniature temperature detection circuit that utilizes a single $60\mu A$ current source and a BMOS inverter, allowing for the detection of both positive and negative temperature changes. With a precision of 0.24°C for each step and an error of ±1.4°C, this design achieves precise temperature measurement in a highly miniaturized form. Furthermore, the proposed design's energy consumption is extremely low at 1.06nJ per transformation, making it suitable for applications in power-constrained environments.

We establish a framework for defining geometric configurations within Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, drawing inspiration from principles outlined in the paper "Geometric Obstructions to Embedding Automorphisms in Symplectic Reductions" by C. Duval, H. Hawkins, R. Wilson, and A. Kh. Bakhtigarov. This framework's key feature is the computation of precise formulas for certain configuration spaces, expressed in terms of the underlying groupoids and stacks. These formulas take the form of explicit equations resulting from applying smooth vector bundle operations and operations within the groupoids and stacks.

We've discovered infrared dark nebulae, specifically DRG, which are undergoing significant star formation including the formation of massive stars. These nebulae, as seen in submillimeter and far-infrared radiation, display dense, cold cores that are gradually being illuminated by young stars formed within them. By analyzing the movements of gas and solid particles, we found that the cores are growing in mass, a crucial finding for understanding massive star formation. Normally, massive stars require a reservoir of gas with sufficient mass to form their protostars quickly. If this process takes too long, the newly formed star may lose its necessary mass and switch to more slowly forming low-mass stars. Consequently, dense, closed systems like DRG are unlikely to see massive star formation. On the other hand, open systems like DRG do have the potential for forming massive stars, as we've observed the presence of young massive protostars in them. Furthermore, we observed a notable increase in the mass of one specific core in DRG over a span of six years, a finding that needs verification but if true would be the first direct evidence of massive star formation in our galaxy.

We establish one-step relation estimates for a wide class of stationary stochastic fields defined by the mean squared error criterion, which is a measure of forecasting accuracy. One-step relations involve finding the best linear predictions for random field values at given locations based on observations from other locations. We derive explicit bounds on the mean squared error of such predictions, which can be used to determine optimal observation configurations for data collection in various applications. These include geostatistical surveys, magnetic field data, and astronomical density estimates of the cosmic microwave background. We also compare our results to existing literature and analyze special cases of wide-sense stationarity and anisotropic fields.

The flow of complex liquids through narrow channels and porous media is influenced by the surface area that they must navigate, which in turn is affected by the composition of the liquid. Studies have shown that while the impact of surface area resistance remains uncertain, it is thought to be significant, especially for highly viscous liquids. This paper investigates the surface area resistance in foam flows, using a controlled setup where foam flows through a single channel and a packed bed of different sizes. By comparing the results with a mathematical model, the importance of surface area resistance was found to be minimal, even for relatively small channels. Rather, other factors such as the clogging of channels by the liquid surface and the breakdown of bubbles due to shear stress were found to have a more substantial impact.

This study develops a 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) to recognize skin carcinomas, with particular attention to distinguishing melanoma from atypical moles. To enhance performance, we apply data augmentation techniques, splitting the augmented data into training and validation sets. This method enables us to remove outlier samples, which negatively affect the accuracy of out-of-sample predictions. After optimizing the network, we use the validated data to train and tune the hyperparameters for an extreme learning machine (ELM) with different activation functions. To determine the final model, we perform a comparison of different ELM variants and find that the model predicting atypical moles includes an outlier class of pagetoid reticulosis. To correct this, we recollect the training data, removing outlier samples from the atypical mole category. With this revised dataset, we retrain the 2D CNN and use it to train and tune the hyperparameters for an ELM with different activation functions. To identify the final model, we compare the performance of different ELM variants, obtaining accurate results for both melanoma and atypical moles.

During a rapid injection of a chemically distinct fluid into a rotating chamber filled with another fluid, a unique pattern of tiny fingers begins to form. This occurrence has been observed in both a stationary and a rotating frame of reference. As the injected fluid's surface tension is altered, the formed fingers become more flexible and take on a curved shape. Additionally, when the chamber is spinning rapidly, the direction of the finger's tip may change, depending on its distance from the injection point. This change in the finger's tip direction is observed when the chamber is spinning quickly enough that the centrifugal force becomes comparable to the surface tension acting on the fluid. This phenomenon has been explained by considering the combination of centrifugal force, surface tension, and the interface's curvature, which results in the fingers' curved shape and their tip's changing direction over time.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers, CCH and CN variants, in the TMC-1 region, using a combination of submillimeter spectral lines observed with the 30 m radio telescope in Nagano, Japan. Isomers, which have the same molecular formula but distinct structures and chemical properties, are rare in space molecular observations. Typically, only one isomer is found and it is often the most stable form. In this groundbreaking discovery, researchers found both the anti and syn isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, with the anti form being the more abundant of the two. By using a laboratory simulation of spectra with varying magnetic fields, they were able to accurately map the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules in space. Further analysis of the data revealed that the cyclopentadiene molecules are more abundant than diacetylene molecules in the TMC-1 region.

In Neural Machine Translation, the task of machine-readable summary creation and full text generation are typically treated as separate problems. Researchers have proposed various methods to generate abstracts, but typically use the same training objective for both summary creation and full text generation. In this study, we test a novel approach where we train two separate neural network models for the two tasks. One model is trained to generate machine-readable summaries with a focus on the first 50 words, while another model is trained to generate the remaining text given this summary. We test this approach on two dataset types: NIST machine paraphrase datasets and CNN/Daily Mail summary datasets. Our results show that for both datasets, generating the full text from a summary outperforms direct generation of the full text. Interestingly, when we use the learned summary as a starting point or "focus" to guide the full text generation, our NMT model prioritizes keeping the same key points mentioned in the summary. This phenomenon we term "look-ahead focus" can be beneficial or detrimental to the generated text, depending on the specific dataset.

The significant discrepancy between computing research and actual problem-solving has motivated scientists to adopt a translational approach. This approach emphasizes taking existing knowledge and applying it to solve real-world challenges. We use the example of grid computing development to demonstrate the effectiveness of a translational method. Specifically, we show how Nelson's speedup function and Friedman and Goodman's knowledge-level analysis successfully guided the development of grid computing by providing a precise measure of computational systems' efficiency in solving real-world problems. As a result, we are able to counter the prevailing concern that research on grid computing failed to achieve significant progress.

A novel combined dark model, known as DCDSM, is proposed where dark matter and dark energy follow the same power-law distribution but with different exponents. This model overcomes the current cosmological crisis by providing a well-fitting solution to observational data, including the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillometry, and the Hubble constant, with a notable improvement in the fit to the mainframe equations.

Using an effective field approach, we investigated the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter plus a photon. This analysis focused on light meson decoupling and revealed permissible ranges for neutrino properties and dark matter's effective coupling. Specifically, we found that the minimum allowable dark matter coupling falls within the 10 to the power of -4 range. Additionally, this analysis indicated that the lightest neutral antiparticle's mass must exceed 0.16 GeV, and we found that the effective neutrino electric current's magnitude cannot exceed 0.25 times the standard electron neutrino's current. Moreover, this approach enabled us to develop accurate estimates for J/ψ decay into light antiparticles and provided a means of distinguishing dark matter's presence based on J/ψ's decay into invisible matter and photon pairs.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) for modeling and decomposing complex time series data embedded within a high-dimensional space. Inspired by the successes of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) in capturing nonlinear dynamics and singular spectrum evaluation (SSE) in representing multivariate functions, MFSSA bridges these two approaches by applying SSE to the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues obtained from MSSA. The resulting MFSSA model exhibits comparable performance to multivariate functional covariance (MFCov) in estimating and reconstructing multivariate time series data. Additionally, MFSSA can be utilized to overcome the dimensionality reduction challenge associated with MFCov. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MFSSA in modeling multivariate financial indices, multivariate temperature fields, and multivariate proxy time series data.

We investigate the long-term behavior of a specific class of random processes with negative drift and finite average duration between consecutive visits to the same level. Our primary focus is on establishing that the processes that spend a significant amount of time near a given level have a similar long-term behavior, as indicated by the eventual likelihood of finding the process at that level. This analysis extends initial results by Darling and Doléans-Darling, Lalem, and Mambou, who constrained the initial condition to a compact interval.

The IShTAR plasma generator at the IPP in Garching is considered a key component for the investigation of the ISOLDE experiment at CERN. To ensure the successful operation of IShTAR in helicon mode, a comprehensive review of its plasma characteristics is necessary. This review focuses on plasma species, charge states, and energy spectra of neutral atoms, as well as particle and energy fluxes. It also addresses the validation of IShTAR in helicon mode for ISOLDE's current and planned experiments.

Nucleus segmentation in histopathology images is a critical and intricate task that can be substantially complex due to overlapping cells, poor staining, and similar cellular textures. To address this challenge, a multi-stage approach has been successful. We propose a novel end-to-end architecture, known as W-Net, which integrates fusion and separation of related tasks to achieve automatic cell nucleus segmentation. In W-Net, two stage tasks are performed in series: a preprocessing stage that performs coarse nucleus segmentation using convolutional neural networks, and a refinement stage that removes oversegementation using the output from the previous stage. The two stages are connected through skip connections to facilitate learning and representation of the image features. Experimental evaluations on provided public datasets and additional acquired datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of W-Net in terms of accuracy and robustness.
We demonstrate the regional converse theorem for several odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups over a semi-local non-compact global field with a specific set of conditions.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained significant traction in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the internal mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a third-generation general relativity framework, where a massless scalar field is present, we derive a modified description of gravity. This modified description involves a Proca field, which allows for the representation of general electrodynamics through a Chern-Simons term. We demonstrate that spinning hairy black hole solutions and solitons can be described within this framework, even when gauge fields are present. Additionally, we show that our model reduces to the standard Einstein field equations in the limit of a vanishing Chern-Simons term, without a massless scalar field.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise computation of tissue displacement caused by sonic pulses. Despite advancements in elastography, errors in shift estimation remain a challenge, particularly in deep tissues. This paper presents a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method to enhance the accuracy of shift estimation near the transducer. VOSA involves the combination of two separate synthetic aperture techniques to account for the varying distance of tissue displacement sources from the sensor. This method enables the construction of a highly detailed and precise displacement map with a small aperture, specifically in the near-field region. Computational simulations using realistic models of human organs demonstrate the superiority of VOSA over conventional synthetic aperture techniques. Furthermore, the feasibility of VOSA is also illustrated through the analysis of actual elastography data. In contrast to conventional synthetic aperture techniques, VOSA exhibits a significant reduction (up to 5 times) in lateral shift estimation errors.

We introduce a new framework called "Rational Pseudocode" (RP) to bridge the gap between mathematical proofs and programming examples shown in lectures. RP aims to provide a way to formally represent the structural content of programming examples, making them compatible with the logical structure of proofs. We achieve this by developing a specific programming language that consists of a limited set of constructs to encode the structure of proofs using programming concepts. We connect RP to the theory of a programming language called "TL" which offers soundness guarantees. To illustrate the capabilities of RP, we utilize it to represent and verify programming examples from various educational sources. These examples, originally written in different programming languages, are successfully re-implemented within the RP framework, demonstrating the versatility of this approach.

In the one-dimensional case, a previous algorithm achieved clustering in $O(\log k)$ time with a data size of $N$ and a similarity matrix of $d$, whereas another algorithm required $O(k \cdot \log N)$ time with the same data parameters. We modified the second algorithm to match the previous result's performance. Additionally, we applied the one-dimensional clustering solution to solve the $k$-means clustering problem dynamically, with the same data parameters, and specified the data and similarity matrix definitions.

We introduce a novel framework for deciding hierarchical strategies in dynamic decision processes with uncertainty, where a higher-level entity makes broad decisions and a lower-level entity refines them, despite having limited knowledge. We call these "superior" and "inferior" decisions high-level and low-level, respectively. A key aspect of this model lies in its ability to accommodate a specific type of uncertainty, which we call "division uncertainty." It arises when the low-level decision's impact on outcomes is only understood in relation to broad high-level decision categories. A key challenge in analyzing these processes is that the low-level decision's effects on outcomes are intertwined with the high-level decision's effects. To tackle this, we develop a new method for assessing the low-level decision's impact on outcomes by categorizing them based on high-level decision categories. By applying this novel approach, we are able to derive a straightforward way to define the low-level decision's distributional distance, which in turn enables the low-level decision's hierarchical learning objective to be re-expressed in a form that is amenable to analysis. We further demonstrate the practical applicability of our framework by applying it to a stochastic pursuit-withdrawal game, which we term the "Hierarchical Stochastic Pursuit-Withdrawal Game" (HSPW). This research focuses on calculating the cross-section of vector boson interactions with muons in the context of the Standard Model, using two methods for a wide range of energies. Initially, the contribution of these interactions is determined for 100 GeV to 10000 GeV energies using the structure function approach, with the resulting equation accounting for the effects of QCD. Alternatively, the cross-section of these interactions is directly estimated for 200 GeV to 20000 GeV energies, factoring in the impact of form factors and electromagnetic interactions. Furthermore, this study compares the outcomes of both methods, presenting the resulting distributions of hadronic decay products induced by these interactions.

In complex systems with interconnected tasks and limited resources, a significant challenge arises from the rapid degradation of performance in just one aspect, which we call "catastrophic disruption." This problem occurs because the optimization of a system for multiple tasks through reinforcement learning often leads to an overreliance on the most easily learned tasks, causing it to poorly perform in a critical area when it's suddenly impaired. In our study, we explored a scenario with multiple, independent tasks that were trained separately using reinforcement learning and found a surprising benefit - the combination of these independent systems actually prevents catastrophic disruption. We call this approach "modularity" and found several ways it could be improved further. Moreover, we applied this modularity to a realistic scenario with multiple tasks and saw a notable improvement in its performance.

We examine the earliest known instances of theories that incorporate a disjunction, making them inconsistent. This exploration leverages propositional logic and first-order arithmetic. In particular, we investigate the presence of such inconsistent theories within the frameworks of classical logic, intuitionistic logic, and second-order arithmetic.

This paper develops a three-spheres theorem for non-zero Dirac-helmholtz measures in the context of Clifford analysis. Specifically, we show that if a function f belongs to a Sobolev space and its support lies within a sphere of radius r in R^n, then the integral of the absolute value of the (k+1)th component of the Dirac-helmholtz operator applied to f, over the k-sphere of radius r, is directly proportional to r to the power of n-2k. This result can be seen as a generalization of a well-known three-spheres theorem from harmonic analysis.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to determine a system's initial state given its current state and parameters that influence its development. These types of problems are known as deconvolution or 'inverse' problems, and they are the opposite of problems like image denoising or super-resolution that aim to enhance a clear image with noise. Real-world applications of this research can be found in fields like using tomography to reconstruct images of the human body. Because direct computation of the initial state is often too computationally expensive, researchers commonly use numerical methods to approximate the initial state. However, these methods require significant computational resources and are typically too costly for high-resolution images. An alternative strategy involves solving the forward problem repeatedly with different initial states to see which one results in the observed data. This method is more efficient but time-consuming because it requires numerous forward problems to be solved and can be problematic when the noise level in the data is high. Recent studies show that generating the initial state with Generative Adversarial Networks generates a realistic representation of the underlying process. But because these models generate the entire probability distribution of possible initial states, they are often too complex and difficult to train accurately. In this research, we present a novel approach that uses a Conditional GAN to reduce the noise in data that has been degraded heavily. Unlike traditional Conditional GANs, the model accounts for the uncertainty in noise estimates and includes a regularized version of the adversarial loss function. This study examines whether symmetry in dynamical systems is preserved when their underlying dynamics changes from a traditional differential equation to a fractional-kernel description. We investigate a representative model with fractional derivatives, obtaining novel solutions that indicate the absence of invariant surfaces within this new framework. As fractional dynamics offer more precise representations of real-world processes, our findings highlight the potential implications for the behavior of these systems.

The interstellar medium is a complex and dynamic medium that allows us to observe the interstellar scintillation of pulsars, which can provide valuable information about the small-scale structure of the medium. Pulsar scintillation patterns can persist for several decades, indicating that the underlying interstellar medium remains relatively stable over this time frame. This discovery encourages us to examine the relationship between the pulsar and the surrounding interstellar medium more closely. By analyzing the patterns of scintillation from the bright pulsar PSR B1133+16 over a twenty-eight-year period, we observe significant changes in the scintillation patterns, which likely result from the motion of the pulsar through the interstellar medium. The data indicate that the pulsar is moving towards a localized density of the interstellar electron gas, which could be causing the increased scattering of the scintillation patterns. However, the absence of notable variations in the width of the scintillation patterns over time suggests that the electron density of the surrounding environment has remained relatively constant during this period. The dimensions of the dense interstellar environment, which can be inferred from the motion of the pulsar, suggest that it may have a major influence on the surrounding solar system, including the Earth, over a timescale of several centuries.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) while efficiently utilizing a smaller amount of training data. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as both the encoder and decoder. However, its applicability is hindered by the excessive computational burden and poor pitch control, necessitating a vast amount of training data. To address these limitations, a compact pitch-independent encoder based on a single dilated convolution layer is proposed, allowing for both reduced computational requirements and improved pitch control when compared to the original WN encoder. Furthermore, the model includes residual connections between the encoder and decoder, enhancing learning efficiency. The generative model incorporates a stochastic process with the recombination technique from WaveNet, combining the output of the encoder with the conditional distribution of the next sample to determine the current sample. The resulting sound wave is obtained by reversing the process used to generate the log magnitude and phase spectrum. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of QPNet in accommodating various pitch ranges and outperforming Wavenet-Synthesis, along with comparable quality to WaveNet-Synthesis in terms of FR and SSR.

Bicategories provide a sophisticated framework for capturing the essence of symmetric monoidal functors and serve as the foundation for higher categories beyond ordinary category theory. A pivotal aspect of bicategories is lacking - namely, the fundamental understanding of subobjects. This gap in knowledge has significant implications, given that subobjects are a fundamental concept in category theory and are directly connected to important principles such as universal properties, first-class citizens in category theory. In seeking to address this shortcoming, we develop a theory of shadows that serve as a bicategorical equivalent of subobjects. Notably, our approach yields a distinctive characterization of strongly fully faithful functors that complements and contrasts with the characteristic provided by universal properties. Furthermore, this characterization enables us to establish a significant equivalence between shadows and marks, a relationship that forms the basis for a bicategorical interpretation of Skolemization.

For individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, obtaining visual information from audio sources is extremely difficult, if not impossible. Despite significant progress in computer vision, there are limited solutions to transpose auditory information into a visual format that can be easily understood. This challenging problem motivates a new task called Auditory-to-Visual Transposition (AVT). In AVT, an algorithm takes auditory signals and maps them to static images that convey equivalent information. We introduce a novel dataset called AVT-100, a 10-class classification problem derived from everyday sounds and everyday activities as seen in YouTube videos. Our proposed approach combines both signal processing and computer vision techniques to accurately classify sounds based on related visual content. We present and compare several models for sound classification and transfer the trained models to the AVT task. Our results show that using convolutional neural networks trained for sound classification and inverse GANs to generate the corresponding images leads to satisfactory performance.

Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a successful AI approach, applying neural network capabilities to complex graph-based data and demonstrating practical applications in various challenging tasks. However, the underlying geometry of graph data, particularly when it is nonlinear and non-Euclidean, remains underexploited. We introduce a novel GNN framework, Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), that leverages the rich theoretical properties and flexible representation capabilities of the Lorentzian space to tackle real-world non-linear, non-Euclidean challenges. In specific cases, LGNN is demonstrated to outperform existing methods, including a globally optimal solution for a particular problem.

Reconstructing a source inside a cavity that's filled with a compressible fluid is an inverse problem that's technically complex and mathematically challenging. This challenge becomes even more substantial when the source and boundary conditions within the fluid-filled cavity are unknown and need to be identified from limited sensor data obtained from the cavity's boundary. This study involves a linear acoustic model, where the goal is to find an inverse solution for a source inside a two-dimensional rectangular cavity that's filled with air, using sensor data collected from the boundary. A Greedy Algorithm is used to recover the source and boundary conditions from noisy data, and the results show that despite the noisy data and a limited number of sensors, the source and boundary conditions can be recovered accurately.

We introduce a new stochastic delay differential equation model, inspired by the Tsallis functional, which includes exponential and fractional components. This novel model allows us to investigate the Tsallis statistics in a dynamic context. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this model and prove its stability in various norms. The Tsallis-inspired exponential delay differential equation model admits a unique solution for certain Banach space norms, and we establish its rate of convergence. Furthermore, we derive the asymptotic properties of the delay differential equation model with fractional components and investigate the conditions under which the model exhibits a fixed point or a periodic attractor.

We construct a type of massive gravity through cosmic string theory's extended Chern-Simon's interaction and demonstrate that a specific harmonic gauge in this framework is necessitated in order to avoid ghost fields and ensure stability. Furthermore, we derive a new Fierz-pauli term that includes higher-order spatial derivatives, and show that this new term behaves as expected under a constant rescaling of the metric. Additionally, we investigate the new term's perturbative corrections to harmonic gravity and find that they yield a type of massive graviton that is consistent with the low-energy spectrum of the underlying theory.

Weyl-Wigner formalism provides a pictorial representation of classical physical systems and their operators. When combined with Wigner-Weyl representation of quantum operators and their classical counterparts, a rich graphical language is employed to illustrate quantum statistical mechanics. This feature allows a direct visual interpretation of the conditions of canonical equilibrium for a quadratic Hamiltonian. The classical version of these conditions, which describe parabolic potential surfaces in phase space, serves as a foundation for understanding the surrounding mini-spheres of initial states that reach canonical equilibrium rapidly. A detailed analysis of the escape time from these spheres in phase space is facilitated by a graphical representation of the Poisson random process. This research took place within the Quantum Thermodynamics and Nonequilibrium Quantum Thermodynamics research groups.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has seen significant development in both theoretical and experimental fields. Initially met with skepticism, the concept now enjoys a more positive reception. The technique of canonical averaging has been found to present a clear, intuitive picture of negative absolute temperatures in both coherent and incoherent systems. This method shows that the condition for negative absolute temperatures boils down to a straightforward inequality between average energy and thermal energy. Consequently, the condition that a system must possess a range of both high and low energy states in order to exhibit negative absolute temperatures has been widely misconstrued. In reality, as we demonstrate with examples of both single and multiple component systems, a system requiring only a minimal amount of energy to transition from positive to negative absolute temperatures can indeed exhibit negative absolute temperatures. Notably, the simplest example of a negative absolute temperature system involves a two-component system with a non-zero interaction energy.

We have developed an effortless scoto-seesaw framework, which requires that the smallest imaginary parts of polarizability operators be no more than half the size of the largest parts. Under this condition, we find that the easiest framework prevents the dominant contribution to electric dipole moment from being significantly enhanced. Moreover, it also prevents the easiest framework from leading to an Ademollo-Nelson suppression of $CP$-even Higgs boson decays into fermions. Additionally, we determine that the easiest framework excludes certain light charged Higgs boson states and includes all possible combinations of light, heavy singlet fields. Consequently, we find that the easiest framework is identical to the minimal dark matter sector that consists of two singlet fields. Within this framework, we find that the easiest framework avoids both the fine-tuning problem of electroweak symmetry breaking and the dark matter overabundance problem. However, it does not avoid the light charged Higgs boson mass logarithmical fine-tuning problem.

We employ a spin-orbitally independent model to examine the transition metal compounds with $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital degeneracy. As these compounds have a large on-site Coulomb repulsion, we account for this effect in our model. When the on-site interaction is large, the model reduces to a two-band Hubbard model, separating $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals. We studied the phase diagrams of these compounds across various conditions, finding that the on-site interaction strongly affects the phases, while the on-site transfer interaction has a weaker influence. Furthermore, we mapped out the phase diagrams for different dimensions and found that the $e_g$ band generally dominates the $t_{2g}$ band due to their differing spatial and orbital symmetries.

This research examines a type of invariant called relative quantum homology for complex, compact surfaces defined by specific equations. It demonstrates that two versions of relative quantum homology are computationally equivalent for surfaces with genus greater than 1, using a particular analytical technique called perturbation theory. Additionally, it shows that relative and absolute quantum homology are computationally equivalent for a specific class of surfaces with genus greater than 1 and particular symmetry properties. Furthermore, it finds that a specific symmetry property, which a particular type of surface lacks, cannot be deduced from the invariants called A-polynomials.

The safety of healthcare workers is paramount, and protecting them from hazardous infectious diseases necessitates rapid and accurate diagnosis. Deep learning-based image analysis has revolutionized medical diagnostics, but training such models on publicly available image datasets poses an infection risk to healthcare professionals. This paper explores a novel concept where partially or fully synthetic chest X-rays are generated to supplement existing training datasets for the Pneumonia-COVID-19 classification task. Our study indicates that combining artificially created images with existing datasets enhances classification performance compared to using real images alone. Specifically, our results show that models trained on a mixture of fully synthetic and real images achieve an F1-score of 0.95, surpassing the performance of models trained solely on real images (F1-score: 0.78) or existing, fully real datasets (F1-score: 0.83). Moreover, our research demonstrates that introducing non-hazardous background noise into real images can significantly improve classification performance, with a 6% improvement in the F1-score.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and analysis. It is capable of mapping high-dimensional data onto a two-dimensional space using non-linear projection techniques such as Self-Organizing Maps. The program includes tools for visualizing data properties and patterns, sorting data objects based on predicted attributes, and graphically examining the structure of data sets. ViDaExpert can be utilized for both beginner-friendly exploratory data analysis and more advanced methodology involving probabilistic modeling and optimization.
